newsitem.title: GERMANY: Airport slot reform unlikely before 98 - EU official.
newsitem.headline: Airport slot reform unlikely before 98 - EU official.

text.p: Reform of rules governing access to slots at European airports is not likely before 1998, a senior European Commission official said.
Ludolf van Hasselt, principal EC transport administrator, said even if the Commission presented a reform plan by June or July, the incoming Luxembourg presidency was not likely to take up the issue.

The issue was "a political hot potato" and Luxembourg had other priorities for its six month presidency in the second half of 1997, he told the 5th Frankfurt Air Travel Symposium at Frankfurt airport.
But he had "no doubt" that the British presidency starting in January 1998 would take up the issue.
Commission officials said on January 21 that proposals were due in February but added two days later that discussions were still under way.
Van Hasselt said the Commission aimed to combine several principles, including respect of existing rights, opportunities for new entrants and the potential for hub expansion.
The proposals would aim to provide "a framework which ensures that a scare resource is allocated in a fair and transparent way", he said.
Strict limitations would be put on any slot trading, van Hasselt stressed.

"One of the most important limitations which we would like is that trading should not be a way to increase your slot portfolio. It should only be a way to facilitate exchanges between carriers," he said.
"We are not discussing Lufthansa, with a lot of money, buying all the slots at Frankfurt and another carrier with less money not getting the slots."
Secondary trading of slots was already taking place at a number of European airports in a "hidden, intransparent way", he stated.

"Should we make it more transparent, should we allow all carriers to take part or should we put a policeman at every airport next to the co-ordinator to make sure that no money is changing hands?" he questioned.
But it was vital to find a system which would meet general industry acceptance, he noted.
"Without a generally accepted system for slot allocation there is the danger that governments would no longer have to negotiate over traffic rights but over airport access," he warned.
